name: The four attitudes (maitrī, pramoda, kāruṇya, mādhyasthya)
method_summary: Cultivating friendliness to all beings ('may no one do evil, may no one suffer, may the world be freed'), joy at the virtues of others, compassion for the afflicted, and impartiality toward the incorrigible; recited in the Sāmāyikapāṭha and used to support meditation.

equivalents.note: same four attitudes; the Jain form assigns each to a class of beings, the Buddhist pervades all directions

name: The five concentrations (pārthivī … tattvabhū)
method_summary: The earth, fire, wind, water and essential concentrations that make up embodied meditation (see prc:pindastha-dhyana).

equivalents.note: burning and dissolving the body by the elements before re-creating a pure body: Jain embodied meditation and Śaiva/Pāñcarātra purification of the elements

name: Placing letters and syllables on the body (nyāsa)
method_summary: In the Devī Gītā's daily worship: placing the letters (mātṛkā-nyāsa) and the syllable hrīṃ (hṛllekhā) in the body.

name: The six-limbed yoga of the Maitrī
method_summary: Breath-control, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, concentration, contemplative reasoning (tarka) and absorption; the text adds placing the mind in the no-mind and the breath in the fourth (6.19), a concentration by restraining speech, mind and breath with a gesture of the tongue at the palate, seeing brahman by tarka (6.20), and rising through the suṣumṇā joined with breath, Om and mind (6.21).

equivalents.note: five limb-names shared; tarka (Maitrī) versus anusmṛti (Buddhist); order and goal differ

name: Mahāmudrā (the great seal)
method_summary: Pressing the perineum with the left heel, the right leg stretched out and its foot held with the hands, the chin on the chest (throat lock), the breath filled and held upward, then released slowly; practised on the left side and then equally on the right (HYP 3.10-15; GS 3.6-8; ŚS 4.16-20; DYŚ 121-122; GŚ 33). The texts say kuṇḍalinī then straightens like a snake struck with a stick and a death-like state arises as the breath leaves the two channels (HYP 3.11-12). It is the first of the trio (with mahābandha and mahāvedha) taught already in the Amṛtasiddhi.

equivalents.note: same name, different practice: a bodily seal in haṭha, the resting of mind in its nature in the Buddhist siddhas
